title: Mating without stalemating
outcomes: Tells checkmate, stalemate and neither apart at a glance
Counts the lone king's legal moves before every move that is not mate
Picks the move that restricts the king but leaves it a legal move, and rejects the stalemating one

steps.text: A winning side can throw the game away in one move. If the lone king is **not in check** and has **no legal move**, the game is a draw by stalemate, however much material you have. So before every move that is not checkmate, ask one question: **after my move, can Black still make a legal move?** The danger is highest on an edge or in a corner.

steps.caption: White to move. Qh3 is checkmate. Qg3 takes away every square without giving check, so it is stalemate and a draw.

line.say: Check along the h-file; the white king covers g1 and g2, so Black has no legal move and is in check: checkmate.

steps.caption: White to move: mate in three, starting with quiet moves (moves that are not checks). Qg5+ and Qh5+ are not stalemate; they simply lose the queen to the king, so they only draw.

line.say: A quiet queen move, a knight's move from the king, with no check.
Another quiet queen move. The white king stays on f3.
The white king guards g4, so the queen mates.

steps.text: **Count the king's moves after your move.** Check and a legal reply: play on. Check and no reply: checkmate. No check and no reply: stalemate. This holds for queen and rook alike. *Rule of thumb:* a quiet queen move a knight's jump from the cornered king often takes the last square, so count first. It is only a guide: the next pair shows it failing.

steps.title: Same queen move, one king step apart
steps.prompt: White plays Qg6 in both. Black's king is on h7 or on h8. Predict the result each time, then check.
Which question did you skip before a quiet move: could Black still move, or was the king in check? What will you ask first next time?
